extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (schools, colleges, universities), Title IX coordinators, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX retaliation definitions and standards
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and definitional standards in the Department of Education's final Title IX rule concerning what constitutes retaliation and peer retaliation, including protected activities, adverse actions, causal connection, exceptions (e.g., compelled participation), and examples/applicability for recipients. Intended to guide recipients' policies, investigations, and responses to alleged retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “Retaliation” (interference and participation clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of “retaliation” at §106.2 includes an “interference” clause and a “participation” clause: the interference clause prohibits an adverse action taken “for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX”; the participation clause applies when an adverse action is taken because a person “has reported information, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing” under the Department's Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation is consistent with longstanding Title VI/IX language and federal case law; the participation clause covers actions like responding to a complaint (so adding “responded to a complaint” would be redundant). The final rule also adds a clarifying sentence that nothing in the definition precludes a recipient from requiring employees or other authorized persons to participate as witnesses or otherwise assist in investigations, proceedings, or hearings under this part. Recipients must treat retaliation claims in light of both clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected activity — scope and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Protected activity includes the exercise of any rights under the final regulations, including procedural rights under §§106.45 and 106.46, and other rights such as a pregnant student's request for reasonable modification under §106.40(b)(3)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of protected activity include making a complaint, appealing a determination under §106.46(i), requesting time off for pregnancy-related medical appointments, or otherwise exercising rights under the regulations. The protected-activity element is informed by the participation and interference clauses and federal case law (e.g., reporting sex-based harassment to school employees is protected activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse action — intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination (materially adverse test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The retaliation definition uses terms like “intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination.” Whether an action is adverse is determined by whether a reasonable person would find the challenged action materially adverse — i.e., it well might have dissuaded a reasonable person from making or supporting a charge of discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply a reasonable-person/materially-adverse test (citing cases such as Burlington and Ollier). Context-specific, fact-specific analysis is required: actions such as lowering grades, making threats, disclosing confidential information, exclusion from programs, adverse hiring/promotional decisions, or assigning harsher duties may constitute adverse actions depending on their impact. Comparators and deviations from policies may be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of confidential or sensitive information may be retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately disclosing or threatening to disclose confidential information about a person (e.g., LGBTQI+ status, pregnancy or related condition) can constitute an adverse action and thus retaliation if taken for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because of participation in Title IX procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients also have obligations under other provisions to protect privacy and confidentiality (§§106.44(j), 106.45(b)(5)). Disclosure as part of an employee reference check may not be retaliation if lawful and not taken for retaliatory purpose; conversely, using confidentiality agreements as prerequisites to accessing rights or supports could constitute retaliation if used to interfere with Title IX rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled participation exception for employees and authorized non-students
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the definition or this part precludes a recipient from requiring an employee or other person authorized by the recipient to provide aid, benefit, or service under the recipient's education program or activity to participate as a witness in, or otherwise assist with, an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarification responds to concerns that a ‘refused to participate’ clause could prevent recipients from compelling employee participation; the Department treats employees differently than students because recipients exercise greater control over employees. Recipients may require certain employees to notify Title IX Coordinators when they have information reasonably constituting sex discrimination (§106.44(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Students may refuse to participate without retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations, a recipient may not retaliate against a student (including an actual or potential complainant, respondent, or witness) for refusing to participate in Title IX grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient may nevertheless investigate and resolve a complaint consistent with its grievance procedures despite a student's refusal to participate; imposing disciplinary sanctions on a respondent after concluding procedures (even if the respondent refused to participate) is not itself retaliation when the decision follows the recipient's grievance process (see §106.46(f)(4)). The exception allowing compelled participation does not extend to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal connection (retaliatory motive) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation requires a causal connection: the adverse action must have been taken “because” an individual engaged in a protected activity or “for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although direct proof of decisionmaker intent may be unavailable, retaliatory motive can be established via direct evidence (e.g., statements) or circumstantial evidence (e.g., changed treatment following protected activity, temporal proximity, disparate treatment, deviation from policies). The Department declines to remove the retaliatory-motive requirement as it has been part of Title IX regulations since 1975 and is supported by case law (e.g., Jackson, Mercy Cath. Med. Ctr.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When non-Title IX processes or additional proceedings may be retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiation of disciplinary processes or filing complaints outside the Title IX context could constitute retaliation if those actions meet the standards in §106.71 and the definition of “retaliation” or “peer retaliation” — i.e., if taken for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because of participation, and if the recipient lacks another non-pretextual reason for the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must evaluate motive and available legitimate reasons; mere parallel proceedings are not per se permitted if motivated by retaliation. Fact-specific analysis required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer retaliation — definition and scope (student-to-student retaliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of “peer retaliation” applies the retaliation standard to student-to-student conduct: conduct undertaken for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because a person participated in Title IX grievance procedures is peer retaliation when engaged in by a student against another student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer retaliation can overlap with sex-based harassment but has different elements. Examples (from NPRM) include teammates vandalizing a complainant's locker or a student council president threatening committee removal for serving as a witness. Recipients must address peer retaliation where conduct reasonably may meet the definition, but are not required to monitor all student interactions (including social media). Recipients are not expected to investigate peer conduct that would not meet the definition of peer retaliation even if proven. Mere criticism or ostracism alone does not necessarily constitute peer retaliation; First Amendment protections remain applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between peer retaliation and sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Although both are forms of sex discrimination, the elements differ: peer retaliation requires conduct taken for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because of participation; sex-based harassment (hostile-environment) requires unwelcome sex-based conduct that is subjectively and objectively offensive and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies access to the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must address conduct that meets either or both definitions. The regulatory obligations for investigating and responding may differ depending on which definition is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: No actual-knowledge/deliberate-indifference threshold for retaliation claims under these regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to impose an actual-knowledge requirement or deliberate-indifference standard for retaliation claims, reasoning that the Supreme Court has not applied such an actual-knowledge requirement to retaliation and consistent with its approach to sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must respond to conduct that reasonably may meet the definition of retaliation/peer retaliation when they have information that such conduct is occurring; the rule does not require proof of actual knowledge in the legal sense used for some other Title IX contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on recipient responsibility for third-party or non-recipient actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to extend the definition of peer retaliation to adults acting on behalf of a student (e.g., parents or guardians) because a recipient may lack control over those actors; however, to the extent a recipient is aware of anyone engaging in harassment or retaliation toward a student, it must respond consistent with §106.44, which might include providing supportive measures or investigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients have obligations when they become aware of harassment/retaliation even if actors are not employees or students; remedies and responses depend on the recipient's level of control and the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements and prerequisites to accessing Title IX rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a student to sign a confidentiality agreement as a prerequisite to obtaining supportive measures, initiating an investigation or informal resolution, resolving a complaint, or exercising any other rights under the final regulations could constitute retaliation if done for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because the student participated in the Title IX process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recipients must take reasonable steps to protect privacy during grievance procedures (§106.45(b)(5)), such protections must not restrict the parties’ ability to obtain and present evidence, consult advisors, or otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures. Conditioning access to rights on confidentiality may be retaliatory in purpose and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory text clarifications and small textual changes affecting application
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific textual clarifications made in the final rule include changing the term “receives” to “has” in §106.71, adding “reasonably” before “may constitute,” adding “under Title IX or this part” after “retaliation,” clarifying that recipients may, as appropriate and consistent with §106.44(k), offer informal resolution in retaliation complaints, and adding “both” before “§§106.45 and 106.46” to clarify consolidation requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These textual changes are intended to align wording across the regulations, broaden the triggering circumstance (has information), require a reasonableness qualifier, and clarify procedural options (informal resolution) and consolidation obligations under the grievance procedures.
